analysis.one_liner: Bans firing, refusing to hire, or otherwise discriminating against workers because of their sexual orientation.
analysis.headline: Despite a Republican lead sponsor and 36 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for employers with 15 or more workers, employment agencies, and labor unions to fire, refuse to hire, or treat workers differently because of their sexual orientation, including an orientation someone merely perceives them to have. It would have enforced this through the same system used for race and sex discrimination claims under the Civil Rights Act of 1964. It carved out religious organizations and the armed forces, barred quotas and affirmative-action remedies, and did not require employers to extend benefits to domestic partners.
analysis.who_benefits: Gay, lesbian, and bisexual workers — and workers perceived as such — who would gain the right to sue for hiring discrimination, firing, harassment in pay and promotions, and retaliation, with the same enforcement machinery and remedies available under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unlawful employment practice for employers with 15 or more employees to refuse to hire, fire, or discriminate in pay, terms, or conditions because of sexual orientation, real or perceived [S3].
Extends the same protections to employment agencies, labor unions, and apprenticeship and training programs [S3].

Gives the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and federal courts the same enforcement powers and remedies used under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, including attorney's fees for prevailing workers [S2][S3].
Bars employers from retaliating against workers who file charges, testify, or assist investigations of sexual-orientation discrimination [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers, unions, and employment agencies would bear the cost of compliance and potential discrimination claims, though the bill rules out quotas, preferential treatment, affirmative-action remedies, and punitive damages, and does not require domestic-partner benefits.

drawbacks.text: Critics argued the bill would expose employers to new lawsuits over hiring and firing decisions, expanding federal litigation risk to every covered workplace [S2].

Religious organizations argued the government should not limit their ability to make employment decisions consistent with their beliefs; the bill granted them a broad exemption, applying only to jobs producing taxable unrelated business income [S3].

The bill had real gaps an honest supporter would acknowledge: it explicitly did not require domestic-partner benefits, barred disparate-impact claims so facially neutral practices could not be challenged by statistics, and excluded the armed forces, meaning gay service members remained subject to the military's policies [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is substantial for the workers it covers — job loss and discrimination are serious harms with no federal remedy at the time — while the cost to employers is bounded: the bill copied the existing Title VII framework, banned quotas and affirmative-action orders, limited damages, and exempted religious organizations, the military, employers with fewer than 15 workers, and domestic-partner benefits. The main fair criticism is not the burden but the design limits: no gender-identity coverage, no domestic-partner benefits requirement, and no disparate-impact claims.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and the Congress ended with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. James Jeffords, a Republican, introduced the Employment Non-Discrimination Act of 1999 on June 24, 1999, joined by 34 other senators listed on the bill [S3][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
36 senators signed on as cosponsors: 34 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a markup, the Senate never voted, and the 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who could continue firing or refusing to hire workers for being gay, lesbian, or bisexual without federal legal exposure, and religious organizations that would have faced new limits. Workers who could still be fired for their sexual orientation gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who could still fire gay workers

for.name: Sen. James M. Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its Senate sponsorship

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or advanced the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended

against.name: Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor schedule and never brought the bill up for a vote

against.name: Religious-conservative organizations
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against the bill, arguing it would restrict the freedom of religious employers

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a bipartisan face — a Republican lead sponsor and 36 cosponsors (34 Democrats, 2 Republicans) — but support ran overwhelmingly Democratic, and with Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and controlling the schedule, the bill never reached the floor.

industries.note: Because the bill never passed, covered employers avoided new federal liability for sexual-orientation discrimination and kept the ability to fire workers for being gay, lesbian, or bisexual. That gain came directly at the cost of a legal protection for workers.

The bill would have exempted religious organizations except for jobs producing taxable unrelated business income, so its death also preserved their full freedom in employment decisions. Religious employers gain here by being able to make decisions workers cannot challenge.
These covered entities also avoided new nondiscrimination obligations and potential claims for referral and membership decisions, which the bill would have imposed.
